title: Jaguar’s Controversial, Production-Ready Type 01 Revealed

body_markdown:
Two years after it broke the internet with the launch of its Type 00 concept car in Miami, Jaguar has returned to the U.S. to reveal the production version of that car, unsurprisingly named the Type 01, at an event in New York. The concept car got a little lost in the social media maelstrom sparked by its unveiling, which focused on Jaguar’s seeming abandonment of nearly 90 years of heritage—just about everyone had a take on it.


The production version’s launch has been delayed by more than a year by a perfect storm of rapidly shifting market conditions for EVs and one of the[costliest cyberattacks in history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaguar_Land_Rover_cyberattack) at JLR. But now, a reborn Jaguar you can actually buy is finally here. Well, almost: Order books for the Type 01 open at the start of 2027, with first deliveries in the second half of the year, if that schedule doesn’t slip again. It will be priced at around £120,000 in its home market, or $160,000 in the U.S., before tariffs and taxes.


And if the Type 01 looks remarkably similar to the Type 00 concept, save for that car’s possibly ill-advised Rhodon Rose pink paint and the fact that this one has four doors, that’s because the production car actually came first and the concept version was developed from it. The car you see here was already waiting in the wings when the storm broke two years ago.


Jaguar


Jaguar


Jaguar


So Jaguar isn’t being brave by maintaining the extraordinary proportions and monolithic surfacing of the concept car: The Type 01 had them first. Its looks are still striking, if no longer shocking, after two long years of looking at them without being able to buy or drive one. And it might need those standout visuals to help re-establish Jaguar as a luxury brand with buyers who are unsure about luxury EVs—and against a formidable array of rivals, many of them also new.


Jaguar


So let’s start with those looks. The bluff upright front end, the long broad flat hood, the low roofline, and the solid glassless tailgate all remain. The huge, 23-inch rims (21s are an optional downgrade) still occupy more than half the height of this long (204-inch) and low (57.5-inch) four-door GT. What Jaguar terms “the luxury gap”—the long stretch of bodywork between the front axle and the point where the A-pillar meets the body—is designed to evoke the powerful front-engined cars of the past and is willfully anachronistic in an EV. It occupies the same proportion of the total length of the car—17%—as it does on the E-Type. A brass-effect “fender ingot” spans the full length of the gap, laser-engraved with the Jaguar leaper.


Jaguar


Jaguar


Jaguar


Heading backwards, the broad square shoulders lend solidity and precision but were remarkably difficult to execute for a production car. The rear three-quarter body pressing is known internally at Jaguar as “the impossible panel” for the way in which the aluminum has to be pressed in five planes and has three feature lines converging at the same point. The rear lamps are hidden behind louvers until activated, and the active aerodynamics also don’t spoil the discipline of the shape until needed, with vanes in the front grille only swiveling open when required, and a pop-up spoiler deploying at speed.


Jaguar


Jaguar


The theme continues in the cabin, which we were shown back in August. A high central spine divides the space into four sections. The driver faces a vast 24-inch OLED screen controlled by a secondary 7-inch smartphone-style touchscreen on the central console, where the driver’s hand naturally falls. Brass is also used inside, along with Kvadrat high-end wool fabric and NeoGrain vegan leather.


Jaguar


Jaguar


Jaguar


Jaguar


With 1016 horsepower and 1006 lb-ft from its tri-motor setup (260kW on the front axle, and two 310kW units on the rear), this is the most powerful road-going Jaguar ever, but the company hasn’t felt the need to pursue a crazy, Lucid Air Sapphire–style sub-2-second time from 0–60 mph. The time of 3.2 seconds Jaguar claims for the 62-mph sprint is[still plenty quick](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/ride-in-the-jaguar-type-00/) enough, and the mere four additional seconds needed to reach 112 mph is probably more impressive. Having ridden in a prototype of the Type 01, we can attest that the acceleration feels appropriate for a Jaguar: imperious but calibrated to never be brutal. We’ll save our final verdict for a drive in a finished production car, but that prototype already used its adaptive air springs to marry the quiet, fluent ride you expect from a Jaguar to impressive body control for a car estimated to weigh 6000 pounds. At least that weight is split exactly evenly across the axles. It feels surprisingly nimble, too, with intelligent torque vectoring across the two rear motors and all-wheel steering combining to make it feel almost mid-engined.


Jaguar


Weight aside, Jaguar has worked hard to counter your objections to luxury EVs before you’ve made them. The huge 118kWh battery gives a 400-mile EPA-rated range, and around 320 miles even when cruising at European highway speeds. JLR’s own customer data, drawn from over 900,000 vehicles in 51 countries, shows that the Type 01’s range is sufficient for 99.7% of journeys. If you do need to stop to charge en route, the car’s 850V electrical architecture and 350kW peak charging speed mean you can add 200 miles of range in just 13 minutes, assuming you can find a charger that fast. And Jaguar, as we know, has gone all-in on electric. The JEA, or Jaguar Electric Architecture platform, which underpins this car and the two SUVs that will follow, has been designed solely for this purpose. There should be none of the compromises involved in retrofitting an EV drivetrain to a platform designed for ICE.


The detail of the Type 00 concept car got a little overlooked in the furore that surrounded its launch. The danger here is that the qualities of the Type 01 will also get overshadowed by the difficult market it is being launched into. The total design and propulsion reboot of Jaguar began in secret more than six years ago, in very different times. Back then, the European Union still intended to ban ICE engines completely, but since then sentiment on EVs has shifted markedly in both Europe and the United States.


Rawdon Glover, managing director of Jaguar, with the all-new Jaguar Type 01.


Jaguar


Buyers remain unconvinced about the merits of luxury EVs, and even the best have seen their sales falter. For all its critical success, the Porsche Taycan is unlikely to survive as a separate nameplate, and its EV replacement is likely to be part of the Porsche Panamera family. The Rolls-Royce Spectre has seen sales halve in a year. Yet we see more luxury EVs arriving all the time—often, like the Type 01, much delayed and conceived when makers were more optimistic about EVs. The Mercedes AMG GT is a new, direct rival for the Type 01, in addition to the Taycan, the[Audi RS e-tron](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/vellum-venom/vellum-venom-2026-audi-rs-e-tron-gt/) , the Lucid Air, and, outside of the U.S., the Lotus Emeya. The related new Jaguar SUVs to follow will see stiff sibling rivalry from the new Range Rover and Range Rover Sport Electric, and from the[Bentley Torcal](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/torque-of-the-town-bentley-unveils-its-first-ev-the-torcal/) , which was revealed late last month. All are competing for a limited and wary group of clients. You have to admire the bravery of the Jaguar reboot, and the boldness of the design and engineering of this first new-era production car, but we worry that Jaguar might lament its timing.
